spatial_claims.claim: D lies on segment BC; AD is perpendicular to BC (constructed via 1.12)
Triangles DBA and DAC adjoin the perpendicular AD and are similar to ABC and to each other (by 6.8)
Angle BDA = angle BAC (right angles); BA subtends the right angle in DBA as BC subtends the right angle in ABC; triangles DBA and ABC are similar figures similarly described upon BA and BC
Angle ADC = angle BAC (right angles); AC subtends the right angle in DAC as BC subtends the right angle in ABC; triangles DAC and ABC are similar figures similarly described upon AC and BC
D on BC and AD divides triangle ABC into exactly DBA and DAC, so area(DBA) + area(DAC) = area(ABC)

configuration_map: Triangle ABC with right angle at A; BC is the hypotenuse. Point D is the foot of the perpendicular from A to BC, lying strictly between B and C. Angle BDA = angle ADC = 90 degrees. Triangle DBA has right angle at D, triangle DAC has right angle at D. Both sub-triangles are similar to ABC by 6.8. Figures P (on BC), Q (on BA), R (on AC) are similar and similarly described. No auxiliary points inside triangles or outside circles; all positions are unambiguous and determined by the single altitude construction.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The proof uses a single standard construction (altitude from right-angle vertex to hypotenuse) producing an unambiguous configuration. The similarity relationships, corresponding-side identifications, and area decomposition all follow correctly. No angle decompositions, no inside/outside ambiguities, and no conflicting point positions arise. The different route via 6.22 instead of Heath's 6.19 introduces no spatial contradictions.
